title: Scoreboard Engineer
objectives: I can create a variable and explain that it stores a value that can change.
I can use a variable to build a working score counter.
I can test my scoring code across several rounds to check it is actually right.
I can use a forever loop to keep my scoreboard on screen, and say how a loop is different from an event.

config.headline: Every game keeps score. Today you build the scorekeeper.
lines: In this lesson you will learn what a VARIABLE is: a named box in the computer's memory, where it keeps something it needs to remember. The box's name never changes. The value inside can change any time. Today your box will hold a number — your score. It is the most useful idea in all of programming, and by the end of the hour you will have built one, changed it, reset it and watched it work.

Look at the photos: the arcade's high-score table, a GAA scoreboard, the step count on a wrist. Behind every one of them is a variable — a box called score, or steps, holding a number that keeps changing.

You will also learn the second SHAPE of code. Lesson 2 was all events — code that sits and waits for a press. Today you add the LOOP: code that never stops. Your scoreboard uses both at once, and by the end you will know which job belongs to which.

And at the end, your scoreboard gets a real job: a whole-class Reaction Rally, scored on the scoreboards you built. You are secretly on a team — nobody finds out who is with who until your teacher reveals the teams at the very end.

config.title: The Scoreboard Ladder
config.intro:
This is where you build it — with the person beside you, one micro:bit shared between the two of you. Three rungs, each one an upgrade. The micro:bit is the judge: the number on its display is either right, or it is lying — and your tests will catch it.

You BOTH build every rung, each on your OWN computer — exactly like last lesson. Talk it through together as you go, and watch the simulator on your own screen: it shows your score the moment your blocks change. You share the real micro:bit for the real test, so take turns. At each rung, one of you downloads the program and drags the file across, while the other presses the buttons and reads the display. Swap over at every rung, so you both do both.

You'll build TWO shapes of code today: an EVENT that sits and waits for a button press, and a LOOP that just keeps going on its own.
config.setupLead: Before rung 1, set MakeCode up like this:
setup: Open MakeCode using the button above. Keep it in its own tab all lesson.

Click New Project, type scoreboard as the project's name, and press Create. Do NOT open your Signal Relay project from last lesson — today's scoreboard is a fresh build. (Missed the name box? Click the box at the bottom that says Untitled and type scoreboard there.)
A blue Welcome box may pop up when the editor opens — click its ✕ to close it. You do not need the tour today.
Build all three rungs in this SAME project. It grows as you climb — you never start another one today.

Every time you press Download it saves a new copy of the WHOLE project, replacing the one from last time. If a box asks whether you want to replace the old file, say yes — that is exactly what you want.

rungs.title: Rung 1 — Wake the Scoreboard
rungs.imgAlt: The finished blocks for rung 1: a forever block with 'show number score' inside it.
rungs.hint: Variables → 'Make a Variable...' → name it score. Do NOT drag a new forever block: every new project already has one (next to 'on start'). From Basic drag 'show number 0' into forever's mouth, then drop the round 'score' block from Variables into the 0 slot so it reads 'show number score'.
rungs.stepsLead: Build exactly what Part 2 showed you:
steps: Make a variable and call it score.
Drag 'show number score' INSIDE the forever block that is already sitting on your canvas.
testSteps: Watch your simulator without pressing anything. It already reads 0 — nobody pressed a button. That is the forever loop starting by itself and showing the number in the box, over and over.

Copy it onto the micro:bit the same way as last lesson: press Download in MakeCode, then drag the file across onto the MICROBIT drive. (If your micro:bit won't connect, keep going on the simulator while your teacher fixes it.)
The real display reads 0 too — your scoreboard is awake.

rungs.title: Rung 2 — Make It Count
rungs.target: Your challenge: make every press of button A count.
rungs.hint: Number stuck at 1 on the micro:bit? First check you downloaded again after the swap — the micro:bit only changes when a new file lands on it. Still stuck after a fresh download? Then the old 'set score to 1' block is still in there — swap it out, don't stack them: 'change score by 1' ADDS one to whatever is in the box.
steps: Add a separate event: 'on button A pressed', with 'set score to 1' inside it.
Press A on the simulator a few times. Watch the display: the number sticks at 1, no matter how many times you press.
Now swap 'set score to 1' for 'change score by 1'.
rungs.note: When you're done, your button A event holds just that one block — the forever loop is still doing all the showing.
testSteps: Press Download and drag the new file across. Your micro:bit keeps running the OLD program until a new file lands on it.
Press A three times. Does the number climb by exactly one per press — 1, 2, 3?

One more proof, on the SIMULATOR: drag 'show number score' OUT of forever and drop it on empty canvas. The simulator's display goes dark and STAYS dark, even when you press its A. No loop — no scoreboard.
Put the block back INSIDE forever. (Your real micro:bit still shows the old copy — it only changes when you download again.)

rungs.title: Rung 3 — The Reset Button

part.label: Part 4 — Reset for a fresh game

rungs.target: Your challenge: give your scoreboard a fresh-start button.
rungs.hint: Reset lives on its OWN event: a separate 'on button B pressed' block with 'set score to 0' inside it. You do NOT need another 'show number score' anywhere — the forever loop already shows every change the moment it happens. Leave your button A blocks alone.
steps: Add a second event: 'on button B pressed'.
rungs.note: When it works: A still counts up, B wipes the score back to 0, and the loop keeps the number on screen the whole time.
testSteps: Download and drag the new file across once more, so the micro:bit holds all three parts of your program.
Press B — it says 0. Press A three times — it says 3. Press B — back to 0.
Now run that whole cycle three times over. A scoreboard that's right once can still be wrong — three clean rounds is proof.

stretch.title: Stretch — The High-Score Keeper
stretch.target: Your stretch challenge: teach your micro:bit to REMEMBER the best score ever.
steps: Make a SECOND variable and call it highScore.
From Logic, drag an 'if … then' block inside 'on shake'.
Set the if's question to: score > highScore. (The > sign means 'is bigger than'.)
Inside the if, put 'set highScore to score'. Now, whenever your score beats the best ever, the best ever is replaced.
Last job — teach the forever loop to show BOTH numbers. After 'show number score', add 'pause (ms) 1000'.
Then add 'show string "H"', then 'show number highScore'.
Finish with one more 'pause (ms) 1000'. The display now takes turns: your score … H … the best score … and round again.
testSteps: Score 3 and shake — after the H you see 3.
Score 5 and shake — after the H you see 5.
Now score just 2 and shake. After the H it STILL says 5? Then your micro:bit officially remembers the best.
stretch.note: That 'if' block is asking a question — you will build lots more of those next lesson.

config.introSolo: This is where you build it — on your own today, so you do every job yourself: build the blocks AND run the multi-round test. Three rungs, each one an upgrade. The micro:bit is the judge — or the on-screen simulator, if there is no micro:bit beside you. You'll build two shapes of code: an EVENT that waits for a button press, and a LOOP that keeps going on its own.
config.help: Each rung starts with its own short video: press play and watch it, then build what it showed in MakeCode (in its own tab), then run the proof steps on the card. Rung 2's break-it step — making the simulator's display go dark on purpose — is part of the proof. The Debug Hint costs 2 XP and points you towards the problem; it never gives the fix away. The film button plays the whole film without losing your place.

config.title: Register your rig
config.intro: In a real rally, every car is checked in before the race starts. Your RIG is your scoreboard program — and this is its check-in. Save it into your Drive, the same way as last lesson. Then, even if a cable is pulled out during the Rally, your work is safe. Press Check my Drive below, and the website will look in your Drive to make sure the file is really there.

steps.title: Download
steps.text: Press the purple Download button in MakeCode — a file called scoreboard.hex lands in Downloads.

steps.title: Vault
steps.text: Open drive.google.com in a new tab. Click into School, then DT Work — the same folder as last lesson.

steps.title: Drag it in
steps.text: Drag the .hex file in. That's it saved — the website will check it is really there.

config.passText: Saved and checked. Your scoreboard follows your login to any machine — and you're ready to compete. The Rally is next.
config.failText: Not registered yet. Check each step — especially that the .hex went INTO DT Work, not just onto the desktop — then press Check my Drive again.
config.help: Download the .hex from MakeCode and drag it into your Drive, in School, then DT Work. Then press Check my Drive — the website really does look in your Drive. It is the same routine as Lesson 2, and it only takes a minute.

config.title: The Reaction Rally
config.intro: Your scoreboard's first real job. You are secretly on a team — nobody knows who's with who until the final reveal. Every point you send in counts for your hidden team.
rules: A rally round: the REFEREE holds the micro:bit where you both can see it, and gives 10 surprise signals — a sharp "NOW!" whenever they like.
The PLAYER holds a finger just above button A. On each "NOW!", the referee calls it: "CATCH!" for a fast reaction, "MISS!" for a slow one. The referee's word is final.
CATCH means the player presses A — the scoreboard they built counts it. MISS means hands off: no press, no point.
Round 1: one of you plays. Round 2: swap jobs. Round 3: the pair chooses who plays the last round.

Press B for a fresh 0 before every round. At the end of a round, read the final number off the micro:bit's display. Enter exactly that number below with the + and − buttons. Your pair's BEST round is the one that counts.
config.confirm: We ran the multi-round test first — B to zero, count up, B to zero, three times, no lies
config.soloIntro: The live Rally happened in class — but your scoreboard still gets its turn. Your catch-up job: prove your scoreboard counts honestly, then play your own rounds and send in your best.
soloRules: Run the multi-round test: B to zero, three presses, B to zero — three full cycles, no lies on the display.
Now a solo round: 10 signals you give yourself — say "now" in your head at random moments, and press A only if you reacted straight away. Referee yourself honestly.
Play three rounds, pressing B for a fresh 0 each time. Read each round's final number off the micro:bit's display and enter it below — your best round still counts for your hidden team.
config.soloConfirm: I ran the multi-round test three times — the scoreboard never lied

suspense.sealed: Teams are SEALED. Nobody in this room knows who they're carrying points for.
suspense.revealTease: Eyes on the big screen — your teacher runs the reveal.

config.help: Follow the five rules on screen. Enter each round's final number with the + and − buttons so it matches your micro:bit's display exactly, tick the promise underneath, then press Send in our score. After that, eyes on the big screen — your teacher runs the reveal.

Enter each round's final number with the + and − buttons so it matches your micro:bit's display exactly, tick the promise underneath, then press Send in my score. The live reveal already happened in class — your points still land with your hidden team.

config.intro: Three questions about today before you go — and these ARE marked: your teacher sees your answers. Think like a scoreboard engineer.

items.stem: In the Rally, a pair press button A five times — five clean catches — but the display says 1 after every single press. What's the MOST likely cause?
options: Their event still has 'set score to 1' inside it instead of 'change score by 1'
The LED display can only show the number 1
They pressed the button too fast

items.stem: A program runs 'set score to 0'. Then 'change score by 1' runs twice. What does 'show number score' display?
Halfway through a rally, the variable named score holds 7. Which sentence is TRUE?
options: The word 'score' will always mean 7 from now on
score currently holds 7 — the very next catch can change it
The program now has seven different scores
7 has become the program's name for score

config.help: Three marked questions about today. Answer them on your own. You find out how you did at the end, after the last screen.

config.intro: Last one. You get four real blocks, and the sentence below describes one working scoreboard. Click the blocks into the order the sentence describes — the loop's job first, then the event's job.

item.prompt: Your scoreboard has two jobs. The first keeps the current score on the LEDs all by itself, over and over, showing whatever number is in the box. The second waits for button A, and adds one to that number every time it is pressed.

config.help: Click blocks from the tray into your program, in the order the sentence describes. Check when you're sure — you'll be shown the working order if it's off.
config.doneText: Correct — that program does exactly what the card asked.
